title: Power Series and Interval of Convergence

sections.heading: Section 1: Finding the Radius of Convergence

questions.q: Find the radius of convergence $R$ for the power series $\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(x - 3)^n}{4^n}$.
What is the radius of convergence of $\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n!}$?
questions.answer: Ratio test: $\lim_{n \to \infty} |\frac{x^{n+1}}{(n+1)!} \frac{n!}{x^n}| = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{|x|}{n+1} = 0 < 1$ for all real $x$. Radius $R = \infty$.

questions.q: Find the radius of convergence of $\sum_{n=1}^\infty n! x^n$.
questions.answer: Ratio test: $\lim_{n \to \infty} (n+1)|x| = \infty$ for any $x \neq 0$. The series converges only at its center $x = 0$, so $R = 0$.

questions.q: Find the complete interval of convergence for $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(x - 2)^n}{n}$.
questions.answer: Ratio test gives radius $R = 1$, open interval $(1, 3)$. At left endpoint $x = 1$: $\sum \frac{(-1)^n}{n}$ converges by AST. At right endpoint $x = 3$: $\sum \frac{1}{n}$ diverges (harmonic). Interval is $[1, 3)$.

questions.q: What is the interval of convergence of $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n^2}$?
questions.answer: Radius $R = 1$. At $x = 1$, $\sum \frac{1}{n^2}$ converges ($p = 2$). At $x = -1$, $\sum \frac{(-1)^n}{n^2}$ converges absolutely. Both endpoints are included: $[-1, 1]$.

questions.q: Why must endpoints always be tested individually when finding the interval of convergence?
choices: The Ratio Test yields $L = 1$ at the boundary points $|x - c| = R$ and is inconclusive
To find the center of the series
questions.answer: Because the Ratio Test limit equals $1$ at $x = c \pm R$, it yields no information at endpoints, necessitating individual convergence tests.

sections.heading: Section 3: Term-by-Term Differentiation of Power Series

questions.q: If $f(x) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n x^n$ has radius of convergence $R$, what is the radius of convergence of its derivative $f'(x) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty n c_n x^{n-1}$?
questions.answer: A fundamental property of power series is that term-by-term differentiation and integration preserve the exact same radius of convergence $R$.

questions.q: Starting from $\frac{1}{1 - x} = \sum_{n=0}^\infty x^n$, find a power series representation for $\frac{1}{(1 - x)^2}$.
questions.answer: Differentiate both sides: $\frac{d}{dx}[\frac{1}{1 - x}] = \frac{1}{(1 - x)^2}$. Differentiating the series term-by-term gives $\sum_{n=1}^\infty n x^{n-1}$.

questions.q: Can endpoint convergence change when a power series is differentiated term-by-term?
choices: Yes, differentiation can lose convergence at an endpoint
questions.answer: While the radius $R$ remains identical, differentiation may cause a previously convergent endpoint to become divergent.
